newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Analysts' views on Brazil's $1 bln March trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Analysts' views on Brazil's $1 bln March trade gap.

text.p: Following are economists' reactions to Brazil's $1.026 billion March trade gap, which takes the nation's first quarter trade deficit to $3.06 billion.

ROBERTO PADOVANI, economist at Trend Analise Economica: "The result for March was a bad sign for imports, which at $4.8 billion were much higher than we expected. This means that April's imports will be about $5 billion, which will give April a $700 million deficit."
Although the government did not give a breakdown of the trade figures, Padovani said increased demand for industrial outputs probably accounted for higher-than expected imports.
Padovani said Brazil would be hard-pressed to post a trade surplus in any month this year, noting that the best result would probably come in May with a $300 million to $400 million deficit.

MARCELO CARVALHO, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Brazil: "It is not a good figure, but it was already expected by the market because the government released weekly trade figures. We are expecting better exports in coming months due to seasonal reasons. But that increase will not offset imports, which will remain strong."

Brazil's agriculture crops are being harvested now and are expected to boost exports through August. But Carvalho said J.P. Morgan isstill forecasting a $13 billion trade gap for all of 1997, up significantly from the $5.5 billion deficit posted last year.

DANY RAPPAPORT, chief economist at MCM Consultores: "This figure was well within expectations during the last two weeks of March, but much higher than earlier forecasts. It suggests imports are still growing due to strong economic activity."
Rappaport said soy and other crop exports over the next three months would bring Brazil's second quarter trade gap to about $1.2 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the first quarter.
MCM forecasts a $9.8 billion trade deficit for 1997, assuming that recent import financing restrictions will cut some $1.2 billion in imports over the remainder of the year, Rappaport said.
